query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Internal residual stresses generated by thermal expansion mismatch during cooling and composite solidification interact with the inherent lattice distortions from multi‐element mixing to control the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. This mechanism postulates that the differential contraction between local compositional regions (or phases) in the nominally single‐phase HfNbTaTiZr HEA produces internal stresses that modify dislocation mobility, thereby affecting tensile creep, microhardness post cold rolling, temperature‐dependent elastic moduli, and age hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy in a single-phase, BCC solid solution state exhibiting inherent lattice distortions from atomic size and modulus mismatches.
generation.intervention: Implement a processing intervention that minimizes thermal expansion mismatch, such as an intermediate annealing or buffering step that promotes homogeneity in thermal expansion properties, and compare these samples with standard processed samples.
generation.conditions: Test across key temperature ranges: high-temperature tensile creep at 1250 °C; microhardness measurements post cold rolling (room temperature conditions); and elastic modulus measurements from 293 K to 1100 K. The aging treatment in the range of 600–800 °C is also examined.
generation.structural_mediator: Internal residual stresses arising from differential thermal contraction (thermal expansion mismatch) in regions with compositional or local modulus variations.
generation.mechanism: During cooling or composite solidification, differences in thermal expansion coefficients among locally distinct regions (even within a single-phase HEA) generate internal residual stresses. These stresses interact with pre-existing lattice distortions, effectively altering dislocation mobility and the Peierls barrier. Consequently, this interaction modifies the alloy’s creep resistance at high temperature, hardness after deformation processing, and elastic moduli, while also influencing aging-induced hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (standard processed samples), the samples processed to minimize thermal expansion mismatch will show reduced internal residual stresses. This reduction should lead to a measurable decrease in yield strength at high temperature (e.g., lower resistance to tensile creep), altered microhardness trends after cold rolling, and a distinct temperature dependence of the elastic moduli. In contrast, samples with more pronounced thermal mismatch are expected to display higher yield stresses and enhanced microhardening due to increased dislocation pinning by residual stresses.
generation.baseline: Standard HfNbTaTiZr HEA samples processed by conventional cooling and aging cycles that develop typical internal residual stresses and exhibit the previously reported tensile creep, microhardness, and elastic modulus behaviors.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is most relevant in the temperature interval where thermal contraction is significant (from the aging range around 600 °C up to creep testing at 1250 °C) and in the regime where the alloy maintains its single-phase BCC structure. Outside these temperature bounds or if additional phases form, other mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports both solid solution strengthening and thermal expansion effects in similar HEAs, the quantitative contribution of thermal expansion mismatch to the overall mechanical behavior in HfNbTaTiZr remains to be determined. The interplay between residual stress effects and intrinsic lattice distortions introduces uncertainty in predicting the exact magnitude of strength changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr HEA samples. The first set is processed under conventional conditions (standard cooling and aging) to develop typical internal residual stresses. The second set undergoes an added thermal homogenization step (via an intermediate annealing or buffering process) aimed at minimizing thermal expansion mismatch. Conduct a series of tests including tensile creep at 1250 °C, post-cold rolling microhardness, and elastic modulus measurements from 293 K to 1100 K while also measuring residual stresses via X-ray diffraction.
measurements: Residual stress profiles using X-ray or neutron diffraction
Elastic modulus as a function of temperature
Thermal expansion coefficient data for each processing route
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention aimed at minimizing thermal expansion mismatch does not produce statistically significant differences in tensile creep behavior, microhardness, or temperature-dependent elastic moduli (and corresponding residual stress measurements) compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch–induced residual stresses are the governing cause for the observed mechanical behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There have been extensive efforts to investigate the strengthening mechanisms in RHEAs (, , ), and the dominant strengthening mechanism in single-phase RHEAs was mostly reported to be the solid solution hardening (). However, unlike conventional alloys, quantifying the effect of solid solution strengthening on HEAs is challenging because of the inability to distinguish between solvent and solute atoms. There are two sources of solid solution hardening in single-phase RHEAs: (i) The random mixing of major alloying elements in the crystal lattice gives rise to local fluctuations and lattice distortions, which introduce energy barriers against dislocation motions and serve as a substitutional solid solution–like strengthening mechanism (); and (ii) Interstitial impurities, such as oxygen and nitrogen, also create high degrees of lattice distortions () and chemical fluctuations, thereby serving as an interstitial solid solution-like strengthening mechanism. AbstractThe synthesis of lightweight yet strong-ductile materials has been an imperative challenge in alloy design. In this study, the CoCrNi-based medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) with added Al and Si were manufactured by vacuum arc melting furnace subsequently followed by cool rolling and anneal process. The mechanical responses of CoCrNiAl0.1Si0.1 MEAs under quasi-static (1 × 10−3 s−1) tensile strength showed that MEAs had an outstanding balance of yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation. The yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation were increased from 480 MPa, 900 MPa, and 58% at 298 K to 700 MPa, 1250 MPa, and 72% at 77 K, respectively. Temperature dependencies of the yield strength and strain hardening were investigated to understand the excellent mechanical performance, considering the contribution of lattice distortions, deformation twins, and microbands. Severe lattice distortions were determined to play a predominant role in the temperature-dependent yield stress.
